To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) a CNN-LSTM-DeCNN framework trained to predict future frames in video sequences achieves excellent performance in visual prediction tasks, (2) the same architecture can be extended to predict out-of-the-plane object rotations, (3) this architecture naturally learns a rich representation of the underlying three-dimensionality of the objects themselves, and (4) this representation generalizes to new tasks, including static image classification.

(1) Predictive Generative Models (PGNs) can be trained to predict future video frames with high fidelity, outperforming state-of-the-art methods; (2) PGNs can be trained to extrapolate out-of-the-plane rotation of 3D faces; and (3) PGNs learn an internal representation of 3D objects which generalizes well to classification of static images.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of deep learning architectures for the purpose of unsupervised learning of high-level visual structure.
the question of whether deep neural networks can be trained to develop an internal model of visual structure, and whether this model can be used to support generalization to novel tasks.
the development and analysis of deep predictive models of visual sequences.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the proposed method is a new way of learning representations of the visual world, and that it is able to do this in a fully unsupervised way, without any labels, and with only a single task: predicting the future.
we have developed an architecture which learns a representation of 3D objects, and that the representation can be used for a variety of tasks, including extrapolation, prediction, and classification.
our model learns a representation of the visual world that allows it to predict future states and generalize across tasks.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have shown that the ability to predict the future states of the world is an effective unsupervised learning task for developing internal representations of the world, and that this can be used as a powerful loss to learn rich internal representations of the latent structure in images.

we show that predictive generative models can be used to learn an internal representation of visual structure that generalizes across a range of tasks and transformations, and can be learned unsupervised from video.

(1) we introduce a novel architecture for predicting future frames of a video sequence; (2) we show that this model is able to learn a representation of 3-D objects from a single view; (3) we show that our architecture is robust to out-of-plane rotations of faces, and (4) we show that the learned representation is useful for other tasks, such as classifying static images.
The main takeaway from our work is that
predictive learning is a powerful unsupervised loss function for learning rich internal representation of high-level object fea-tures.
the ability to predict future frames of video can serve as an unsupervised loss that encourages learning of a rich internal representation of the underlying three dimensional structure of the world.
prediction is a strong unsupervised learning signal that can be used to develop a rich representation of the visual world. * 11 pages, 6 figures, submitted to IC
